# PREFACE.

When I composed my *Historical Essay on St. Jacques de la Boucherie*, <note>St. Jacques de la Boucherie was a prominent parish church in Paris. Today, only its Gothic tower—the Tour Saint-Jacques—remains standing.</note> I had occasion to speak of Nicolas Flamel, a figure as famous for the ideas people have held about his fortune as for the use he made of it.

The natural leaning that people have toward the marvelous has prevented most writers who have mentioned Flamel from examining what was said about him with attention. Without evaluating his foundations <note>In this context, "foundations" refers to charitable endowments, such as the building of hospitals, houses for the poor, and chapels.</note>, they have simply counted them; and judging them more considerable even than those made by Kings and Princes*, they sought their source in means either opposed to integrity or so extraordinary that they border on the miraculous. <note>Villain is referring to the legend that Flamel discovered the "Philosopher's Stone" and created gold through alchemy.</note>

Although at heart it is of relatively little importance to know whether Flamel was rich or not, or if he possessed the

# FOREWORD.

When I composed my *Historical Essay on St. Jacques de la Boucherie* <note>Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie was a parish church in Paris. Most of the church was demolished in 1797 during the French Revolution, but its famous bell tower, the Tour Saint-Jacques, still stands today.</note>, I had occasion to speak of Nicolas Flamel, a figure as famous for the ideas people have held regarding his fortune as for the use he made of it.

The natural leaning that people have toward the marvelous has not permitted most of the writers who have mentioned Flamel to examine with care what was being told of him. Without evaluating his foundations <note>In this context, "foundations" refers to charitable endowments, such as hospitals, chapels, and houses for the poor, which Flamel established.</note>, they have simply counted them; and, judging them to be more substantial than even those established by Kings and Princes; * they have sought their source in means that are either contrary to integrity or so extraordinary as to border on the miraculous.

Although, at heart, it is of relatively little importance to know whether Flamel was rich or not, or whether he possessed the

The husband and wife both enjoyed maintaining a public image, though their tastes in this regard differed. The wife seems to have lived as a proper <term>bourgeoise</term> <note>A 'bourgeoise' was a woman of the comfortable middle class, typically living in a city and holding certain legal status.</note>. Along with this, she possessed a wardrobe quite well-stocked for a time when the luxuries of our own age were unknown. She had contracted debts referred to in one legal act as *the claims and debts of the late Pernelle* <note>original: "les clamis & dettes d'icelle feue Pernelle"</note>. This was perhaps the result of her excessive spending.

After Pernelle’s death, Flamel lived in a different style: more secluded at home with his servant Marguerite *la Quesnel*, and perhaps Collette, the daughter of this domestic worker. ...an abundant mine; he drew from it not only enough to increase his acquisitions, but also enough to provide for the buildings he erected.

Everything he did had religion as its goal. It seems that his outward appearance suggested the greatest simplicity. His statue, which stood at <term>Sainte-Geneviève-des-Ardents</term> <note>A parish church on the Île de la Cité in Paris, demolished in 1747; Flamel was one of its most famous patrons.</note>, appears to show him as such: this is what made him loved. He was gentle in his social dealings and not very demanding in his acquisitions. Perhaps, too, his simple exterior masked a bit of shrewdness; I seemed to perceive some traits of it, but the reader shall judge for themselves.

While he was modest at home, eating, it is said, very common food off earthenware dishes, he stood out through many public works. These made his reputation, even during his lifetime—yet did that reputation not go far beyond his own intentions?

Did Flamel think that a few buildings and his will would establish him as one of the most famous <term>Hermetic Philosophers</term> <note>A historical term for alchemists, referring to the legendary founder of the craft, Hermes Trismegistus.</note>? He has found a prominent place in that class; but did he deserve it? Did he seek and find the admirable and envied secret of <term>transmuting</term> <note>The alchemical process of changing base metals, like lead, into noble metals, like gold.</note> metals into gold? This does not seem credible. He was too rich to have worked, for more than twenty-four years, at a work where one infallibly ruins oneself, when one

However, when I stated in the *Essay on the History of the Parish of Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie* that *one must not look for the source of Flamel's riches in the fable of the transmutation of metals into gold*; I did not intend to deny what those knowledgeable in chemistry believe—that it might not be impossible to succeed in this operation. ### CHAPTER II.

*Of Flamel’s marriage to Pernelle: they bring wealth to one another. Of the profession of Scrivener in Flamel’s time.*

Flamel was intelligent in the management of his affairs; the state of ease he attained is proof of this. Young and clever, he managed to secure as his wife Pernelle, who, although already of a certain age and the widow of two husbands, was wealthy, or at least well-off for her time and station. No official record indicates the year in which these two spouses contracted their marriage:

It seems, however, that in 1372 they could not have been married for very long. A mutual gift, which is the first of the documents they have left us, *(a)* states that the gift is made *because of the great and agreeable services that one brings to the other, since the celebration of their marriage, and continues to bring now.* But in the year 1386, another Act which renews this gift states that they make it to each other because they consider the great goods... services, that for a long time they have done for one another. More than thirteen years had passed since their first Act; thus, in the second, they speak of a "long time," unlike in the first.

The Art of Writing, far from being an unprofitable trade—as stated by the author of the letter I just cited—must have been advantageous at that time. Without repeating the little I wrote on this subject in the *Essay* <note>Refers to the author's previous work, *Essai sur l’histoire de Paris*, which provided historical context for medieval trades.</note>, it is sufficient to consider only the writings necessary for the course of Justice: <term>Memoirs</term> <note>Legal briefs or statements of facts used in court.</note>, Petitions, accounts, etc. How many printers are employed today when cases are pursued with heat in the Courts? All these pieces were brought to the Scriveners, who often produced multiple copies of them; numerous items specified in the old registers as paid to these Scriveners bear witness to this. It was, therefore, a means for them to profit. Add to this the other branches of their profession, such as copies of books or other pieces of writing for the great number of individuals who did not know how to handle a pen.

<margin>Ess[ay], p. 146, 248.</margin>

# OF NICOLAS FLAMEL.

When the art of writing ceased to be cultivated—to such an extent that ignorance of this Art had even become a mark of nobility <note>In the medieval period, many nobles viewed literacy as a technical skill for the lower classes or clergy, rather than a necessary pursuit for a knight</note>—men who were not concerned with this "point of honor" found in the talent of penmanship an advantageous resource for their livelihood. The practice became established, and the people grew accustomed to seeking them there. The example of Flamel, and that provided to us by other Scribes, shows that no matter how wealthy they became, they always retained these places.

Certainly, if our writer were the author of this fine story, he would not have fallen into a blunder that confuses one year with another. As a writer accustomed to copying documents, and perhaps to composing them, he knew the style <note>original: "style" — referring to the specific conventions of administrative dating and formatting.</note>. To avoid this confusion, care was taken at the time to specify in legal acts made between March 22nd, the earliest date for Easter, and April 25th, the latest date for this feast, whether the act was made before or after Easter [*a*], because this great feast regulated the year, and being movable, one would have taken one year for another, as in the case in question: for if the second projection is from April 25th, 1382, the first must necessarily have been done in 1381. But the narrative expressly states for the first: *January 1382*.

All this has thus seated the Writer <note>referring to Flamel's profession as a public scribe or *écrivain*</note> on the Gallic Parnassus <note>a metaphorical reference to the home of the Muses, representing the canon of great French poets</note> alongside Jean de Meun <note>original: "Jean de Méhun," a famous 13th-century poet and author of the *Romance of the Rose*</note> (*c*). But here is a prejudice well-founded, it seems, against the reality of this Gothic muse. One recalls the little couplet written on a pillar of the bourgeois’s <note>referring to Flamel as a member of the comfortable middle class</note> house. Flamel, as I have said, <margin>See above, page 7.</margin> could have gone to look for it at the Palace <note>The Palais de Justice in Paris, where many public inscriptions were found</note>, where it could be read long before his time. Would such a famous Poet have gone elsewhere to pick up two small verses to decorate his own house? One knows these types of geniuses; they are too susceptible to the point of honor to cover themselves so publicly in borrowed laurels.

Flamel was a Poet in the same manner as he was a painter. He borrows, as we have read, a foreign hand to paint in his home on a delicate occasion where he himself should have worked; when he wishes to versify for his house, he goes again to borrow. It must have been the same with the rhymes of the charnel house <note>the Cemetery of the Innocents</note> that we have just read; they must be the work of some rhymer of the time. The wealthy bourgeois, who loved to show off, no doubt paid well those who worked for him.

Whatever the case may be regarding Flamel's poetry, which with a certain spirit,

### CHAPTER VI.

->*Flamel and Pernelle make a mutual gift to one another, which they renew several times.*<-

The reciprocal love of the two spouses, and the solicitude they had for one another, prompted them early on to bestow upon each other a mutual gift <term>don mutuel: a legal contract where spouses grant their property to whichever one survives the other</term>. I indicated this from the beginning of this work: but the acts of this kind which they subsequently performed to cement this first operation <note>The author uses the word "opération," which typically refers to a legal transaction here, but for readers of alchemy, it also alludes to the stages of the "Great Work"</note>, and with which we are now going to occupy ourselves, require a level of detail into which I shall now enter.

Pernelle was of a certain age. The husband and wife, united for several years, saw themselves without children: they therefore thought to secure for one another not only the wealth they had already acquired in their community of property <note>In French law, "communauté de biens" refers to the joint ownership of assets between spouses</note>, and that which they hoped to acquire *by the pleasure of God and through their own good diligence*, but also that which they had acquired before their marriage. A single object occupied them in that first agreement: it was the affection they bore for one another. In this one, another motive makes them act: works of piety. They give the entire share of the first to die to the *Churches*, to the *poor*, and to *wretched persons*; and this portion must be employed by the survivor, either during their lifetime or by their will, as they see fit.

On the occasion of this new Church, the small village of Menuls, composed of forty houses, where there was already a chapel dedicated to Saint Jemme, was detached from the parish of Auteuil. It therefore appears certain that the Church of Boulogne-les-Menuls is a monument to the piety of a King of France, of Princes, of Lords, and of other members of the brotherhood at the beginning of the 14th century, and that it was built and perhaps finished nearly a century before Flamel's death. This Writer either did not yet exist, or was not in a position to place himself among the noble and illustrious company that had it erected. What he might have done in his time, as a fellow member, may be reduced to the exact payment of brotherhood dues for his share and for 그that of the devout Pernelle <note>Perenelle Flamel (d. 1397), Nicolas Flamel's wife and supposed partner in his alchemical work.</note>: if he did anything more, it was perhaps some gift of such little consequence that it was not thought necessary to mention it.

Nevertheless, one can see today in the Church of Boulogne, near Paris, a monument that may have come from Flamel. It is a figure of the Apostle St. James, placed in the Chapel on the right. This statue was once at the portal of Sainte-Geneviève-des-Ardents <note>A church formerly located on the Île de la Cité in Paris; "des Ardents" refers to a miraculous cure of "Saint Anthony's Fire" or ergotism attributed to the saint.</note>: a private individual purchased it during the demolition of that church in 1747 and had the devotion to have it placed where it now stands.

In fact, in 1399—the second year of his widowhood—Flamel was far from being able to apply himself to a work of reflection such as the hermetic <term>Hermetic: Relating to the mystical and alchemical tradition associated with Hermes Trismegistus.</term> treatise attributed to him. As the executor of his wife’s will, he had specifically taken *upon and on himself the weight, charge, diligence, and care* <note>original: "en & sur soy le fais" — A legal phrasing common in the 14th century meaning he took personal responsibility for the obligations.</note> of fulfilling its conditions. <margin>From a deed dated Jan. 19, 1397-98.</margin> A considerable number of legal acts passed after the death of Pernelle prove evidently that this widowed man, besides his ordinary work, was burdened with many cares. In 1398, one finds transactions, rulings from the Châtelet <note>The Châtelet was the seat of the provost and the primary center of justice and police in medieval Paris.</note>, and a considerable number of *enfaisinements* <term>Enfaisinement: A specialized legal term in old Parisian custom regarding the formal recording or transfer of property rights and land tenures.</term>. In 1399, there is the accounting of the execution of Pernelle’s will; an extensive declaration of the assets of this estate—assets divided into a multitude of very small parts—and other documents, all of which were produced under his eyes and by his care. Amidst such complications, could Flamel have applied himself to composing a work that required a man who was tranquil and free from all business?

Then he could naturally say: *after the passing of my faithful companion whom I shall regret all the days of my life*. But after seventeen years of widowhood, regrets, though real, are no longer of the same vivacity.

If the nephew *Colin* <note>Nicolas Flamel’s nephew, who in later alchemical lore was said to be the recipient of his uncle's secrets.</note> was dear to Flamel, he should have given him his confidence, as he had given it to Aunt Pernelle <note>Perenelle Flamel (d. 1397), Nicolas’s wife and supposed collaborator in his alchemical quest.</note>, and led him step by step through this so risky operation. No: he presents him with a work that even the most skilled do not understand; a sealed work, for which he keeps the key, and he says to him: *work: I have marked as you will mark when opening, as I shall tell you in this book that I present to you*: thus Colin, despite all the friendship of his uncle, is condemned by that very uncle to make at least a thousand blunders <note>original: "mil brouilleries"; failed experiments or confusing errors in the alchemical process.</note>, just as the uncle himself had done, wandering through the long span of twenty-five years, and perhaps becoming a miserable puffer <term>puffer (souffleur): a derogatory term for amateur alchemists who mindlessly blew their bellows at the furnace without understanding the true science or theory.</term>, destined...

The history of a private individual whose obscure life was confined within a small circle of domestic affairs should not provide points sharp enough to greatly interest a Reader: such was Flamel. His life was, strictly speaking, only a sequence of common actions, few of which have even reached us. The only buildings that this Scrivener <note>Original: "Ecrivain." In the 14th century, this title referred to a professional scribe or notary who copied documents and kept records.</note> erected, and his charitable foundations, have made him famous and form his history. This is primarily what will occupy us in this part, where we shall follow him from his widowhood until the time he died. The man, being regarded as extraordinary, will make these details interesting.

Having become a widower, he acted perhaps with more freedom: but he always did so with more ease.

Fontaine, a native of Hainaut, published a work entitled *The Fountain of Lovers of Science* <note>original: "La Fontaine des amoureux de Science," a famous alchemical poem written in the 15th century.</note>.

<margin>The same source.</margin>
Other books of this kind could also appear, such as the *Philosophical Summary*, etc. And the bookseller, being quite shrewd, would not have failed—given the disposition of people's minds—to supply his shop with these books and to sell them all the more dearly, as those who bought them already believed themselves to be in possession of a plentiful gold mine. Might it not be a specific trade in these works that established the foundations of Flamel’s reputation in Alchemy? The bookseller would naturally speak to his customers of the wonders contained in the books he sold: He sold at a high price, and in that, he was a "successful alchemist"; while he abandoned his buyers to the smoke of their lamps <note>A common historical trope referring to the soot and futility of "puffers," or amateur alchemists who spent their fortunes on charcoal and furnaces.</note>, they provided him with very real silver.

(*a*) This fragment is on a piece of paper that wrapped the seal of an act of amortization <term>acte d'amortissement: a legal deed allowing the transfer of property to "dead hands," usually the Church, exempting it from future taxes</term> dated from the year 1411. The state in which I found the seal and its envelope, tied with parchment strips whose knots were very tight and flattened, provided me with proof that it had not yet been unfolded. I submitted the fragment to the expertise of the Reverend Father Dom *Taffin*, one of the authors of the *Nouveau traité de diplomatique* <note>A definitive 18th-century treatise on the study of ancient documents and handwriting</note>. This Reverend Father recognized it as being from the time of Flamel, both by the character of the handwriting and particularly by the "i"s, which are barred across the top instead of the dot we use today. To preserve the seals of his deeds, Flamel had wrapped them in whatever paper came to hand. I found several other seals in the same state. One was wrapped with a small fragment of writing that appears to be from one of the first copies of his will.

One can still see the distress Flamel felt regarding the tax demanded of him. He speaks naturally there, since it is not a formal petition in which he might have tried to deceive a Magistrate; it is advice sought from a friend to whom he reveals his true situation. ### CHAPTER VII.

->*Lawsuits that Flamel initiates and does not finish. His death.*<-

Flamel was approaching his end, and always focused either on preserving and defending the assets he had acquired, or on increasing them according to the common weakness of old men; he lacked neither business matters nor lawsuits. Perhaps these distracting occupations troubled him more than he wished. Nevertheless, some facts seem to show that they were not entirely alien to his taste, and that he knew how to profit from them; and that by purchasing annuities <note>The "rente" was a common financial arrangement in pre-revolutionary France, where an investor provided capital in exchange for annual payments secured against property—effectively a mortgage-like investment.</note> placed on dilapidated properties, (*a*) he found ways—

Regardless, the Bookseller <note>Referring to Flamel, whose primary profession was as a scribe and manuscript seller.</note>, three years before his death, undertook, among others, a lawsuit that he did not see to its end; his testamentary executors completed it.

The subject of the lawsuit was a minor matter. It concerned five *sols parisis* <term>Sols parisis: A unit of currency minted in Paris, worth twenty-five percent more than the standard Tours currency.</term> of rent secured against a house belonging to a man named *Robin Violette*, located on the Rue du Temple at the corner of the Rue des Gravilliers. Later, he likewise held a house located at the corner of the Rue du Cimetière Saint-Nicolas <note>The Street of the Cemetery of Saint Nicholas.</note>, for which a great number of legal acts exist. Flamel purchased a life annuity <note>original: "à droit viage" — a legal right to income or property that lasts only for the duration of the holder's life.</note> of 2 *livres parisis* on this house in 1385, for the sum of eleven *livres tournois*. This annuity was held in his name and that of Pernelle <note>Pernelle Flamel (d. 1397), Nicolas's wife and close collaborator in his business affairs.</note>. After Pernelle’s death, Flamel acquired *the permanent ownership of this rent in 1400*, for 12 *livres* and 10 *sols tournois*, which he paid *with one écu and one gold noble* <term>Gold noble: A high-purity gold coin of English origin, widely circulated in France during the Hundred Years' War.</term>, and the remainder in *blans* <term>Blans (or blancs): Silver-alloy coins, so named for their white appearance, worth eight deniers each.</term> of 8 *deniers* apiece. He then put the house up for public auction <note>original: "criées" — literally "cries," referring to the public announcement of property sales during legal foreclosure.</note>, and it was awarded to him. In 1414, he ceded the ownership of the said house to Jean Perrier, a Mercer <note>A dealer in fine fabrics and textiles.</note>, for the price of the rents that were mortgaged upon it, while reserving his own rights. Perrier sold the site or uninhabited house in 1415 to Andrieu le Prince, a Barber and Valet-de-chambre to the King. Flamel, however, had put it up for auction once again; and Andry Marchant, the Provost of Paris, awarded it to him on the Tuesday after Trinity Sunday in 1414. The matter ended there for Flamel, and Perrier regained the property, which eventually passed to the parish council <note>original: "fabrique" — the administrative body of a parish church responsible for its finances and upkeep.</note> of Saint-Jacques because Perrier failed to "furnish" the house—that is, to meet the financial obligations and charges. One could provide several more examples of these activities of Flamel, and the nearly constant lawsuits he maintained for the management of his estate.

The rent is not free; it is given for the purpose of a Mass which must be celebrated every year in St. Jacques <note>Saint-Jacques-la-Boucherie, the parish church of Nicolas Flamel in Paris.</note>, by a Chaplain from each of these places. Is it not obvious that this Decree, which was carried out, is the source of the rumor that spread that Flamel had founded and endowed fourteen Churches and as many Hospitals? The will, significant in itself, by which the Testator gave all his property to the Church, caused a stir. It was commented upon; additions were made to it. How many inflated accounts, stories tailored by lively and creative imaginations do we not hear every day? People spoke of the fourteen Churches and Hospitals that the Writer <note>Flamel’s actual profession was that of a public scribe or "écrivain."</note> had favored with a foundation. The accountants of the Church of St. Jacques wrote it among their expense items: <margin>From the accounts of 1445 and others.</margin> *Other outlays for fourteen Low Masses <term>Low Mass|A simplified form of the Catholic Mass celebrated by a priest with minimal ceremony and no choir.</term> ordered to be said.... in the month of November in the said Church at the Altar of St. Clement by the people of the Churches and Hospitals declared hereafter, etc.* Every year this quite remarkable troupe of Chaplains reappeared. Yet how many people were ignorant of what was true in the foundation?

# PART THREE.

## CHAPTER ONE.
### *Conclusion of the execution of Pernelle’s Will.*

If we believe that the Reader might take an interest in the facts that will be presented in the third Part of the History of Flamel, it is always with the reservation that most of these facts only become curious because of the great distance from which they stand in relation to us. More than three centuries <note>At the time this text was written, the author is looking back from the 18th century to Flamel’s life in the late 14th and early 15th centuries.</note> is a considerable amount of time: manners and customs have changed greatly. One often reads accounts of very simple things from travelers with satisfaction: the distance of the location gives them merit; "reverence is greater from a distance," <note>original: *major è longinquo reverentia*</note> says Tacitus. Might the same not be true for what we are about to explore? The customs of our Ancestors, and events that took place long ago in the land where we now live, will be for us like those of a foreign region; perhaps they will even interest us further.

It is a sad consequence of all that we call wealth that it occasions disputes and troubles. We have been witnesses to those that arose upon Pernelle’s death between the brother-in-law and the sister-in-law. Whatever care had been taken to firmly establish Pernelle’s foundation, it proved weak in its most essential part. The income <term>rentes</term> <note>Annual payments from investments or property intended to fund the foundation's activities.</note> that had been assigned to it were, for the most part, **established** <margin>From the transfer contract, in 1444.</margin> **after heavy obligations** <note>original: "après grant charges" — a legal term indicating that the income was already burdened by prior debts or liens.</note>; and like almost all those left by Flamel, in a short time **the greater part became worthless** <note>original: "la plus grant partie vint à non valoir"</note>, and the properties from which they were drawn fell into ruin. The Lorimers <term>Lormiers</term> <note>A guild of craftsmen who made metal parts for horses’ harnesses, such as bits and spurs.</note>, seeing this decay and perhaps fearing it would grow even worse in the future, wished to discharge themselves of the responsibility twenty-four years after entering the contract.

It had been decreed that if the Confraternity of Saint Leu was moved out of the Church or annulled and abandoned, the Parish Priest <term>Curé</term> of Saint-Jacques and the Church Board <term>la Fabrique</term> <note>The administrative body responsible for the financial and material maintenance of the parish church.</note> would see that the services were celebrated. It is missing from the sequence of accounts, and leaves a gap of seven years: this is precisely the time during which the orders of the will were being carried out.

<margin>From an account of the execution.</margin>

### CHAPTER IV.

->*The first Executors of Flamel’s will troubled: a criminal lawsuit is brought against them.*<-

Jacques Lamban, Provost of Paris <note>The Provost was the city's primary judge and administrator, representing the King's authority</note>, when granting the release <term>main-levée: a legal order lifting a seizure or attachment of property</term> of the seizure made on Flamel's assets, had ruled, as has been said, that the testamentary Executors would render a full account, and the remainder <note>original Latin: *& reliqua*; refers to the balance of the estate left over after debts and specific legacies are paid</note> before Master Cauthele, the Examiner. The object that was the seed of the dispute and the Lawsuit <term>Procès: the formal legal proceedings regarding the audit of Flamel’s charitable and personal estate</term> was an omission that the Executors, it was said, had made in their account. Furthermore, it must be remembered that the mandates established by the will for a single payment, or for a limited time, could only be fulfilled gradually and, for the most part, through the collection of recurring revenues. Therefore, regarding the total capital that Flamel left behind, it is not a matter of considering everything spent for these mandates; the debt recoveries and the movable property <note>personal possessions as opposed to real estate</note> could only produce a small portion of it. One must focus only on the revenues left by the Scrivener <note>Nicolas Flamel, whose primary profession was a public scribe and notary</note>, as well as the movable goods found at his home and certain debt collections; and this is what will provide the insight we seek.

-># CRITICAL HISTORY#<-

It has been said that these Legatees <note>individuals or entities designated to receive a legacy or inheritance</note> only reached their settlement after an examination of the entire matter that one might call rigorous, "having seen and considered," according to the terms of their contract, "with great diligence the will, business, and affairs of the said deceased" <note>original: "ayant vu & advisé... à grant diligence les testament, besongnes & affaires d'icellui deffunt"</note>. Well-informed people, such as the Cathedral Chapter, a company of Monks, and the Parish Notables <note>prominent or high-ranking citizens of a parish</note>, saw the execution clearly and did not rely solely on the word of the Testamentary Executors. Their terms clearly state that everything was laid out on the table: the will, the inventory, the contracts, the debts—whether collected or yet to be collected—and the reimbursements. The result of such an exact review was the fear that if the assets were divided into quarters, "the deceased might be and remain defrauded of his good purpose, will, and intention, etc." <note>original: "le deffunt ne soit & demeure deffraudé de son bon propos, voulenté & intention, &c."</note>. This is to say clearly that if the division proposed by the three Legatees had been followed, there would not have remained a sufficient fund for the fulfillment of the perpetual foundations <note>endowments intended to fund specific religious services or charitable works in perpetuity</note> with which the *Fabrique* <term>the administrative body or fund dedicated to the maintenance and construction of a parish church</term> of Saint-Jacques was to be charged.

These Legatees respected the memory of the deceased and his will—whether expressed or presumed—which took precedence over their private interests; they set an example that one might perhaps find difficult to follow today.

Four entire chapters of the account are dedicated to the affairs of the estate. The first of these chapters, the fourth of the account, details the receipts from <term>mortgaged annuities: regular income payments (rentes) secured against property assets</term> on houses and locations in *Paris*; the second concerns those established on properties outside of *Paris*; the third is for the rents of the stall and houses in Paris; the fourth contains transfers or reimbursements. On this occasion, those rendering the account enter into a detail that one might call meticulous. This is because, at that time, a straightforward account was given for everything: they were drawn up as much for the instruction of those who followed as for the discharge <note>original: "décharge," a legal release from financial responsibility once an audit is successfully completed</note> of those who rendered them. These details are nonetheless advantageous; they provide these registers with a historical quality from which we derive great use. In this one, as

### OF NICOLAS FLAMEL.
M

this means and by combining his annual earnings with an already established income, as well as the share of the mutual gift <note>The "don mutuel" was a legal agreement between Flamel and his wife Pernelle, allowing the survivor to enjoy their joint property.</note> which he enjoyed, he could have found himself in a position to provide for these expenses. We have seen that he made these expenditures over many years; added to this is the fact that he worked at a time when—whatever proportion one might find between that era and our own—at the very least, one worked more cheaply then than now. Let us add that Flamel had incurred debts; he mentions them himself in his testament: and wills and ordains, he says, <margin>Testament, page 277.</margin> *all his debts to be paid without delay.* This was not merely a standard legal clause, as the account rendered to Commissioner Le Preux expressly stated the aforementioned *outlay*... <margin>The *outlay* [la mise] is what is called "expenditure" in accounts today.</margin> *of the debts that he (Flamel) owed.* Thus, this legal act confirms the reality of these debts, which were satisfied, and the debts indicate clearly enough that the good Scribe <note>Nicolas Flamel's professional title was "Ecrivain," referring to his work as a scrivener and legal copyist.</note>, carried away by his charitable character, did not always consult his financial means. This is what our illustrious witnesses have said above: Flamel did more than the assets and revenues of his estate were worth.

<page-num>286</page-num>

# CRITICAL HISTORY

->Rue St. Martin, the Hostel of the Red Apple, at the corner of Rue au Maire<-, (<gloss>in front of the St. Martin Staging Area <note>original: "Eschielle," which could refer to a set of stairs or a nearby pillory/ladder associated with the Priory of St. Martin-des-Champs</note>, according to the accounts of 1457 to 1458.</gloss>)

(This is a house that Flamel never personally owned, nor did he hold any mortgage <note>original: "rente," a financial arrangement where a property provides a fixed annual income to the holder of the deed</note> secured against it. It concerns the settlement of Pernelle’s estate; thus, it is a supplement to the Founder's own income, which we include here along with several others that have <margin>See folio page 17.</margin> been noted.

The Lormiers <note>a family of craftsmen, specifically makers of metal parts for horse harnesses</note>, who, as previously mentioned, sold the portion of the house from Pernelle’s share, purchased an annual rent of 8 Parisian pounds <note>original: "livres parisis," a currency worth 25% more than the more common "livres tournois"</note> in 1429 from Marie, widow of *Jean de Hoden, a Sworn Bookseller of the University* <note>a prestigious status granted by the University of Paris to certain booksellers, placing them under university legal protection</note>. This rent was mortgaged against this house of the Red Apple.

In the agreement these individuals made with the Parish Works Council <note>original: "la Fabrique," the administrative body responsible for a church's finances and maintenance</note> in 1444, they transferred these 8 pounds to them. Subsequently, the Parish Council purchased several other rents secured by the same house. One can find one for 5 Parisian pounds and another for 1 Parisian pound. *(a)* And in the deed of sale or redemption made in 1452, the Churchwardens <note>original: "Marguilliers," lay officials who managed the parish's temporal affairs</note> are called the Holders and Owners of the house; however, ten years prior, around 1442, *Perrin Germain and his wife Marie* were its possessors. Perhaps the Churchwardens had put it up for public auction <note>original: "criées," a legal process for selling property to pay off debts</note>.)

(In the accounts we are following, this house is said to have been) in great ruin and desolation, such that no one could stay or live there.

Malaquin, Sergeant-at-Arms <note>original: "Sergent à Verge," a type of judicial officer carrying a wand/staff as a symbol of authority</note>, was commissioned for the repairs. Then the said Hostel was leased with the consent of the Churchwardens,

---

*(a) This second rent had been given to Perette la Piloise, a poor Christian woman residing in Paris at the "Dog Pit," otherwise known as Béthisy. The person who delivered the gift was Master Jehan Aguenin, President of the Parliament, acting as the Executor for the late Lord Jehan de Dampmartin, who in life was an Alderman and Burgess of Paris.*

After the long excerpt that has just been read, another matter that might still be of interest is the fate eventually suffered by a number of the <term>rents</term><note>In this period, *rentes* were perpetual annuities or fixed incomes generated by property, often bequeathed to religious institutions to fund specific masses or charities.</note> about which nothing has been said. First, she, as a good and true Catholic, devoutly recommended and recommends her soul, when it shall depart from her body, to the Blessed Trinity of Paradise, the glorious Virgin Mary, to Lord St. Michael the Archangel, to Mr. St. Peter, St. Paul, St. James, and to Lady St. Catherine, and to all the Saints of the blessed and celestial Court of Paradise. *Item.* She willed and ordained her <term>funeral lighting</term><note>Wax candles used during the funeral service to honor the deceased.</note> to be made on the day of her funeral with thirty-two pounds of wax.

*Item.* She left to the four **Mendicant Orders** in Paris <note>Religious orders whose members originally lived by begging; they were central to urban spiritual life in medieval Paris.</note>, that is to say, the **Cordeliers** <note>Franciscans</note>, **Jacobins** <note>Dominicans</note>, **Carmelites**, and **Augustinians**, to each of these four Orders, 6 <term>sols parisis</term><note>The "Parisian shilling," a common medieval French currency.</note> to say vigils for her soul.

<margin>To Wit.</margin> Let it be known that, whereas in several streets of the land and jurisdiction of the said Church <note>Likely the Priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, which held significant land in this part of Paris.</note>, which used to be populated by good, hardworking householders, there is now a great quantity of houses and places fallen into ruin and abandonment, uninhabited for lack of good Owners; because of which there has been for a long time in those streets a great stench of mud and other filth, to the detriment of the guests and householders in the said land. And especially in the **rue de Montmorency**, quite near the old gate called the **St. Martin gate**, there are several houses and lean-tos fallen into ruin, where people day by day create and bring stenches and filth, so much so that it turns to the great grief and prejudice of the neighbors; and because of this, several Rent-holders <note>original: "Cenfiers" — those entitled to collect 'cens' or feudal land rents.</note> have lost the rents they used to take from these houses and lean-tos. And among these houses thus abandoned, **Nicolas Flamel**, Scrivener, had and has a small lean-to, or place similarly fallen into abandonment and ruin, containing about twenty-four feet square within the work <note>original: "dedens euvre" — likely meaning the internal floor area.</note>, charged with one <term>denier|a small medieval copper or silver coin</term> of ground rent per year toward the said Church; bordering on one side a house which has long been in ruin, where formerly there were <term>bathhouses|eftuves</term>, which belonged to the late **Arnoul Cousin**; and on the other side to small lodgings which are likewise abandoned, which belonged to the late **Jehan Delavallée** and **Marie** his wife, abutting at the back the property of **Berthelemy Croquemeure** and **Jehanne** his wife, in her name. The which **Nicolas Flamel** has requested of us that we be willing to <term>amortize|admortir — a legal process to transfer property into "mortmain" (the dead hand), usually for charitable or church use, exempting it from future feudal taxes</term> and free forever this place, to build there an edifice in the manner of a **Hospital**, or otherwise: either **alms-houses** <note>original: "maifons d'aumofne"</note> for poor householders to live in, or to sell this edifice freely, to charge it with rents, to give it to Churches or Hospitals for them to enjoy; or to deliver them by their hands for poor people to live in, or to do with and ordain them by testament...

### ADDITION for page 37.

We add here, for the satisfaction of those who love antiquities, several inscriptions read on the small portal of <term>St. James<note>Refers to the Church of Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie in Paris, of which only the tower remains today.</note></term>, at the same time as the one reported on page 37.

Flamel, who lived across from this small door, took pleasure in decorating it. There is reason to believe that he viewed the collection of all the devotional images he had carved as an <term>oratory<note>A small chapel or space designated for private prayer and devotion.</note></term> intended to be always before his eyes. He had it adorned with paintings, and even gilding, the vestiges of which still shine. The whole was enclosed by a glass window, the frame of which remains entirely intact.

The image of the Holy Virgin, which is in the middle of this small monument, was sculpted with considerable delicacy for the time. She carries the infant Jesus in her right hand, and in her left, she holds a cluster of grapes. This image is supported by two seated angels, whom the Builder <note>Meaning the patron who commissioned the work, Nicolas Flamel.</note> may have intended to represent as singing a hymn in honor of the Holy Virgin; a hymn whose words can be read on a scroll they unfold.

->Behold the Mother of God, Queen of Heaven,<-
->This is the salvation of the human race.<-
<note>Original Latin: "Ecce Mater Dei, Regina Cœlorum, Ista salus humani generis."</note>

In the angles formed by the pointed arch <note>original: *ogive*</note>, two other Angels each raise a censer.

St. James, Patron of the Parish, is on the right side, and Flamel can be seen kneeling at his feet. Pernelle is on the other side at the feet of the Holy Precursor <note>St. John the Baptist, who preceded Jesus.</note>, who is designated by a circle in which the Lamb is depicted, with which this Saint is usually represented. The husband and wife invoke the Holy Virgin; the husband through these words: *Holy Mary, intercede for the people* <note>original: "Sancta Maria, intercede pro populo"</note>. And the wife by saying: *Holy Virgin Mary, pray for us* <note>original: "Sancta Virgo Maria, ora pro nobis"</note>.

<margin>* These figures could not be shown on the vignette on the first page, which only represents the top of the portal.</margin>Four small figures dressed in long robes can be seen outside and under the lintel of the door. * They also hold scrolls, of which the writing of only two could be read, the others being very small and in darkness. It appears that all these scrolls together contain the first two articles of the Apostles' Creed. The first begins: *I believe in God....* <note>original: "Credo in Deum...."</note> and the last carries the words: *Our Lord* <note>original: "Dominum nostrum"</note>; those in the middle undoubtedly contain what lies between the two.

Under the lintel are written on each side two pieces of advice given to those who enter the Church. They are told on one hand: *Keep yourselves in devotion*; and on the other: *Have true contrition*.

<margin>Essay, p. 150 & 151.</margin>There are still several other inscriptions; we have provided them in the *Essay*; they can be read there. All together, joined with the pious images, they characterize the benefactor. Could he have hidden the art of the <term>Great Work<note>In alchemy, the "Great Work" (*magnum opus*) refers to the successful creation of the philosopher's stone, capable of turning lead into gold.</note></term> under these devotional coverings? If someone had imagined embroidering upon this quantity of figures and legends, perhaps we would have a volume similar to that of the explanation of the *Figures of the Charnel House* <note>A famous alchemical text attributed to Flamel describing the symbolic frescoes he commissioned for the Cemetery of the Innocents.</note>. Ordinary eyes see nothing there but what is simple, devout, and in the taste of those centuries, and we presume that nothing more will be seen there.

### *Other Additions & Corrections.*

<margin>See 3rd Part, Critical History, Volume IV, page 233 and following.</margin>
The account of the great lawsuit which arose concerning Flamel's estate has provided the opportunity to speak of Jean Paris, a Proctor at the Parlement <note>A legal representative or attorney in the high court of the Ancien Régime.</note>. This legal practitioner and advisor to the Parish of Saint-Jacques, where he was highly influential, owned a house burdened by *Jean Turquam* with an annuity of 15 livres for certain services. It was the very house where Turquam had lived. Paris, who while managing the affairs of his Parish did not forget his own, wished to free himself from this debt and had the <term>marregliers: lay officials or churchwardens responsible for the financial administration and maintenance of a parish</term> ordered, according to Royal ordinances, to permit the redemption of the annuity for 180 Parisian livres. This is what is recorded in the accounts from 1426 to 1432.

<margin>page 98.</margin>
It should be noted that this house belonging to Jean Turquam, of which Paris had become the owner, is not the one acquired by the Marcel family, as was stated in the *Essay*; it was believed to have been identified in the manuscript memoirs of Monsieur Prévost, a lawyer. Our new examination of the accounts has revealed the truth of the matter. In an entry where the redemption made by Paris is indicated, the Turquam house is described as being on Saint-Jacques-de-la-Boucherie Street, across from *The Three Maidens* <note>original: "les trois Pucelles"</note>, thus on the opposite side from the Marcel house, and facing that of *The Three Maidens*, a house or manor mentioned in our *Essay*.

<margin>Essay, page 74 & see the plan at letter V.</margin>
The inscription which was on Turquam's tomb, removed in 1511 through the efforts of the Examiners at the Châtelet <note>The Châtelet was the headquarters of the Provost of Paris and the city's main court and prison.</note>, can no longer be read today. It read: *Here lies an honorable and discreet person, Master Jean Turquam, in his lifetime Examiner at the Châtelet of Paris, and Criminal Lieutenant of the Provost of Paris, who passed away*

Regarding the foundation of religious services—namely, a solemn Requiem Mass and Vigils of the Dead each month—two legal acts were drawn up, though not until 1410. The first, dated Tuesday, October 21, concerns an annuity of 12 Parisian livres <note>The "livre parisis" was a specific currency unit used in Paris, worth 1.25 times the "livre tournois."</note> left to the Church by Master Jehan Turquant, to be drawn from the house where he lived, located in the Vannerie <note>The "Vannerie" refers to the Rue de la Vannerie, or the street of the basket-makers.</note>. *(a)* This established the services. ### APPROBATION.

I have read, by order of My Lord the Chancellor, the *Critical History of Nicolas Flamel*, etc., and it seemed to me that this curious writing could not fail to be favorably received by the Public, since it concerns a famous man of whom there have been no reliable memoirs until now. The research that the industrious Author has conducted has enabled him to make Flamel known for what he truly was, and to show that the philosopher's stone <note>The <term>philosopher's stone</term> was a legendary substance in alchemy believed to be capable of turning base metals into gold and granting eternal life.</note> attributed to him is a chimera <note>In this context, a "chimera" refers to a wild illusion or a mythological impossibility.</note>. The documents <note>Original: "pieces." Here, the term refers to the primary sources and legal records appended to the historical narrative.</note> he has added may also satisfy those who enjoy learning about the Topography of old Paris. At Paris, August 8, 1760.

->B O N A M Y.<-

### ROYAL PRIVILEGE.
<note>Original: "Privilege du Roi." This was a legal document granting an author or publisher the exclusive right to print and sell a work, effectively acting as both a copyright and a mark of state approval.</note>

LOUIS, by the grace of God, King of France and Navarre: To our beloved and loyal Councilors, the People holding our Courts of Parliament, Masters of Requests ordinary of our Household, Great Council, Provost of Paris, Bailiffs, Seneschals, their Civil Lieutenants, and others of our Justices to whom it shall concern, GREETINGS. Our beloved GUILLAUME NICOLAS DESPREZ, Our Printer

<summary>This page contains the official approval from the royal censor, Bonamy, who praises the author for debunking the alchemical myths of Nicolas Flamel, followed by the start of the Royal Privilege granting publishing rights.</summary>

ordinary [Printer] and Bookseller in Paris, has informed us that he desires to have printed and given to the Public a Work entitled, *Critical History of Nicolas Flamel & of Pernelle his wife*, by Mr. L. V. <note>These initials likely refer to the author, Abbé Nicolas Lenglet Du Fresnoy, a prolific historical scholar and bibliographer of the era.</note> should we be pleased to grant him our Letters of Permission necessary for this. For these reasons, wishing to treat the Petitioner favorably, We have permitted and do permit by these Presents, him to have said Work printed as many times as he shall see fit, and to sell it, have it sold, and distributed throughout our Kingdom, during the time of *three consecutive years*, counting from the day of the date of these Presents. We forbid all Printers, Booksellers, and other persons of whatever quality and condition they may be, from introducing any foreign printing <note>This clause was intended to prevent "pirated" editions printed outside of France (often in the Netherlands or Switzerland) from entering the French market and undermining the official publisher's monopoly.</note> into any place under our jurisdiction: Provided that these Presents shall be registered in full on the Register of the Guild <note>Original: "Communauté." Royal grants often mandated material quality to ensure that French books remained prestigious and legible.</note>, in accordance with the printed sheet attached as a sample under the counter-seal of these Presents; that the Petitioner <term>Petitioner</term><note>Original: "l'Impétrant." that, one [copy] in that of our Louvre Palace, and one in that of our said very dear and faithful Knight, Chancellor of France, the Lord Delamoignon <note>Guillaume de Lamoignon de Malesherbes (1721–1794) was the magistrate in charge of the royal library and the censorship of the book trade; he was known for his relatively liberal administration of the press.</note>; all upon penalty of nullity of these Presents. ->LE BEGUE.<-
